title: Hold a mail drop box's spring-shut hopper open, lay three letters in, then let it shut so its return posts them
instruction: Post the three letters from the letter rack in the drop box, and leave its hopper shut.
context: Mailing a letter at a collection box is an everyday errand: the Postal Service has more than 140,000 blue collection boxes, and hopper collection boxes such as Florence's 4C11S-HOP finish off banks of wall mailboxes. A 1996 patent on the Postal Service's 1170/K box notes that its handle leaves the opening hand under the door, so "the second hand" makes the deposit. Here the door is a hopper hinged at its foot. Pulled open against its springs, it is a V that closes off the box; let go, it swings shut, its floor tips into the box and the letters slide inside. So one hand holds the hopper steady while the other takes three thin envelopes from a rack and lays them wholly in over the door, and only then lets it back; a letter not wholly in when it shuts is not posted. Unlike putting envelopes in a mailbox (BEHAVIOR-1K mailing_letters), the receptacle moves, must be held, delivers the letters itself and must be left shut.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), heights above the table top. Drop box: full-size mock of the hopper section of a Florence versatile 4C collection box (4C11S-HOP, drawing 4C11S-HOPCS): 3/4 in plywood face 44.5 (17 1/2 in) wide and 34 high at x 42, middle at y 0; hopper opening 30.5 wide, 9.6 to 28 up; compartment behind it 30.5 (12 in) wide, 38.1 (15 in) deep, as drawn. Hinge: 3/8 in rod 9 up, 1.2 in front of the face, in two pillow blocks on the face. Hopper: 1/4 in plywood door 33 wide, 20 (7.9 in) hinge to top edge, overlapping the opening; floor 28.9 (11 3/8 in) wide glued along the door's foot, 3.8 level then 14 down into the box at 34 degrees; hardboard cheeks; 0.70 kg. Pulled, its top swings out and down to a stop at 45 degrees; open, it is a V between door and floor; shut, the floor slopes 34 degrees into the box. Curved back: 1/4 in hardboard fixed in the box, its inner face on an 18 radius round the hinge from above the opening to 10 degrees below level; from 20 to 45 degrees open the floor's end lies about 6 mm from it, so the open hopper is closed off from the compartment; shut, the floor's end is below it. Springs: two Lee Spring LTR070M01S torsion springs on the rod (6.998 lb-in at 90 degrees each), wound 40 degrees at shut: 0.70 N m shut, 1.49 N m at the stop. Handle: an Amerock BP40517 bar pull (128 mm centers, 187 long, 13 mm bar 35 mm proud) level across the door, its top 1.5 under the door's top edge. Letters: three #10 envelopes (Quality Park 11112, 9 1/2 x 4 1/8 in, 24 lb), each with one 20 lb sheet folded in thirds, about 10 g and 0.6 mm thick, standing together on their long edge in the 1 cm slot of a plywood letter rack (27 long, walls 4 high) at x 30, y 30, leaning about 12 degrees, stamp corner up and to the robot's right. The box and the rack are fixed to the table. Both arms start at their home poses. Mock vs unit (README): mounted at table height, compartment only 34 high, a cabinet bar pull at the unit's handle place, closing by named springs, no anti-fish comb, plywood not aluminum.
scoring: An envelope is in when it is wholly inside the box (every corner behind the face's back plane and inside the side walls, back, floor and top), at rest, with no part of either arm within 5 mm of it (a release check). An envelope that comes down on the table or the floor outside the box (its middle outside the box's footprint and a corner within 4 mm of the table top or below it) counts for nothing for the rest of the trial, even if posted afterwards; standing in the rack is not on the table. The hopper is shut within 0.8 degrees of closed (its top edge within 4 mm of the face). Score: 0.25 for each envelope that is in, at most 0.5 while the hopper is not shut; 1.0 when all three are in and the hopper is shut and let go (released: no part of either arm within 5 mm of its door or handle, a release check), held 1 s (the trial ends). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Doing nothing scores 0. Envelopes in the open hopper's V in front of the face do not count; ones slid past the face onto the open hopper's floor count, but the score stays at most 0.5 until the hopper is shut. Real trial, in this order: a 4 mm drill bit at the hopper's top edge (shut if it does not go in) and the side video for hands off; the side and overhead videos for any envelope touching the table or floor outside the box during the trial; then the box's back unscrewed to count the envelopes inside.
reset_notes: About 3 minutes with the checks: letters back standing in the rack's slot, hopper shut, the box's back screwed on. Before each trial: a luggage scale on the middle of the handle's bar, pulled square to the door, reads 4.5 to 6 N as the hopper leaves shut and 6.5 to 8.5 N at its stop; let go from the stop or from 10 degrees open, it shuts by itself and a 4 mm drill bit does not go in at its top edge; the three letters weigh 30 g (within 2 g), sealed, uncreased and flat (a spare set replaces any that is not); box and rack on their taped marks. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at full size. The hopper's two torsion springs are PhysX's joint drive at their rated stiffness and preload; its stops at shut and 45 degrees are joint limits. The handle, envelopes, rack and curved back act by real contact only (friction 0.4/0.3; the letters slide off the shut floor for any friction under 0.67). The envelopes are rigid plates of real size and weight. The mock's compartment is lower than the unit's.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps; the letters stayed in the rack and the hopper stayed shut); demo: 1.0 (782 steps)
